n: As Jacob heads home, angels of God meet him. Angels marked his departure from Canaan at Bethel, and now they mark his return.

f.w: the angels of God met him

n: Jacob recognizes God’s army and names the place Mahanaim, “two camps”—God’s camp and his own.

f.g: Means “two camps.” It later became a town east of the Jordan (2 Samuel 2:8).

n: Jacob sends messengers ahead to Esau, who now lives in Seir, the land of Edom. Twenty years after fleeing, Jacob must face his brother.

f.g: The mountainous region south of the Dead Sea, later Edom’s homeland.

n: Jacob instructs them to call Esau “my lord” and himself “thy servant.” Jacob humbly reverses the blessing that made him lord over his brother.
Jacob mentions his wealth—perhaps to show he is not coming to claim Esau’s inheritance—and seeks Esau’s favor.

f.w: that I may find grace in thy sight
f.g: That you may look on me with favor.

n: The messengers report that Esau is coming with four hundred men—an alarming number that sounds like an army.
Terrified, Jacob splits his people and animals into two camps—echoing the name Mahanaim.

f.g: Two camps, the same word as in Mahanaim.

n: If Esau attacks one camp, the other might escape. Jacob plans carefully—and then he prays.

f.w: the other company which is left shall escape

n: Jacob prays to the God of his fathers, reminding the Lord of His command to return and His promise to do him good. This is the first long prayer recorded in the Bible.
Jacob humbly admits he is unworthy of God’s kindness and faithfulness. He crossed the Jordan with only a staff; now he has two camps.

f.w: I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies

n: Jacob honestly pleads for rescue from Esau, fearing for his wives and children.

f.g: An image of total destruction (compare Hosea 10:14).

n: He reminds God of His promise of countless descendants. Praying God’s promises back to Him is an act of faith.

f.w: as the sand of the sea

n: Jacob spends the night there and selects a large gift for Esau from his flocks.

f.g: Hebrew minḥah—a gift or tribute, also the word for an offering.

n: The gift is lavish: hundreds of goats and sheep.
It also includes camels, cattle, and donkeys—over 550 animals in all, a fortune.
Jacob sends each herd separately with a gap between, so Esau will meet gift after gift.
He instructs the lead servant what to say when Esau asks whose animals these are.
The servant is to say they are a gift from Esau’s servant Jacob, who is following behind.

f.g: Jacob consistently calls himself Esau’s servant.

n: Jacob gives the same instructions to every servant leading a herd.
Jacob hopes to soothe Esau’s anger with gifts before seeing him face to face. The word “face” repeats through this passage, preparing for Peniel, “face of God.”

f.g: Literally “cover his face”—related to the Hebrew word for atonement (kipper).
“Face” appears several times here, building to Peniel (verse 30).

n: The gifts go ahead, and Jacob stays in the camp that night.
That night Jacob takes his wives, maidservants, and eleven sons across the ford of the Jabbok River.

f.g: A crossing on the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan. Jabbok sounds like Hebrew ’avaq, “wrestle.”
Benjamin is not yet born; Dinah is not counted here.

n: He sends everything he has across the stream.

Left alone, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious man until dawn. Jacob has struggled all his life—with Esau, with Laban—and now he wrestles with God’s messenger. Enos later describes his own “wrestle” before God in prayer.
When the man cannot overcome Jacob, he touches Jacob’s hip and dislocates it. Jacob will carry a permanent reminder of this encounter.
The man asks to go as dawn breaks, but Jacob refuses unless he is blessed. Jacob, now weak, clings rather than fights—and seeks a blessing from God rather than by trickery.

f.w: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me

n: The man asks Jacob’s name. When Jacob last gave his name to receive a blessing, he lied (27:19). Now he answers honestly: “Jacob”—“heel-grabber.”
Jacob receives a new name: Israel, because he has striven with God and with men and prevailed. The name of a man becomes the name of a people.

f.g: Probably “God strives” or “he strives with God”; also understood as “one who prevails with God.”

f.w: as a prince hast thou power

n: Jacob asks the man’s name but is not told. Instead, the man blesses him there.

f.w: Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?

n: Jacob names the place Peniel, “face of God,” because he has seen God face to face and lived.

f.w: I have seen God face to face

n: The sun rises as Jacob limps past Penuel. A new day dawns for a changed man.

f.g: A variant spelling of Peniel; later a town (Judges 8:8).

n: Israelites traditionally avoid eating the thigh sinew of animals, remembering this event.

f.g: Often identified as the sciatic nerve; still avoided in Jewish dietary practice.
